newsitem.title: UK: Allied Domecq to study Guinness merger.
newsitem.headline: Allied Domecq to study Guinness merger.

text.p: British liquor company Allied Domecq Plc said Tuesday it was studying whether the planned $15.8 billion merger between rivals Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc will give them an unfair dominance in any of Allied's markets.
"We have set up a task force to look at the issue," Allied Chairman Sir Christopher Hogg said in an interview.
Hogg, however, was optimistic about the prospects for his company after the merger, which was announced on Monday and would be the biggest ever in Britain.

"I think we are in a very good position following yesterday's merger, we have 12 of the top 100 brands, we are in increasingly good shape in wines and spirits and we can seize oppurtunities open to us which will be greatly increased by the merger," he said.
Allied shares rose 19.5 pence (31.8 cents) to 466 pence ($7.60) as investors took a view that the group was now more vulnerable to a takeover in the wake of its rivals' merger.
Some investors believe the merger leaves Allied looking weak and in need of strategic partners if it is to stop its market share from being eroded.
Hogg said it was too early to say whether Allied would complain to monopoly authorities about the planned merger. "There is so much to be examined and analysed."
"We have to look at it on a market by market, territory by territory basis. But we have a duty to complain if it's in shareholders interests," he said.
Allied also said pretax profits were little change at 317 million pounds ($515 million), with profits from its spirits and wine division off 2 percent.

The proposed Guinness-Grand Met merger would create the world's seventh largest branded food and drinks company, GMG Brands. It will be the leading spirits and wine group with combined annual sales of more than 100 million cases.
The deal is subject to European Union and U.S. regulatory approval.

Top officials at Guinness and Grand Met said on Monday they did not expect opposition from regulators although Canadian-based Seagram Co. Ltd., the world's second largest spirits company, called the deal anti-competitive.
